Juveniles of the Dusky slug, Arion subfuscus, emerge from the egg mass with a remarkably modest initial mass; at an ambient temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], field-collected neonates typically display a wet weight at birth of 0.02 grams [Wwb = 0.02 grams], a value that underscores their extreme altriciality relative to other terrestrial gastropods. This minimal starting mass necessitates a prolonged period of rapid somatic growth before the animal can attain the body size required for the onset of gametogenic activity. The developmental trajectory from hatching to sexual maturation is strongly temperature-dependent, with the accrual of structural tissue proceeding steadily under constant thermal regimes. The ultimate wet weight an adult individual can achieve, reaching 10.8 grams [Wwi = 10.8 grams], represents the asymptotic body size characteristic of reproductively mature individuals in this population, a figure that aligns closely with published accounts for Arion species occupying comparable temperate niches. This combination of a diminutive birth weight and a substantial adult mass implies a pronounced growth multiplier over the course of the animal's life, requiring efficient assimilation and conversion of ingested plant detritus and fungal material throughout the active feeding months.

Laboratory rearing trials conducted at a stable temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C] have provided precise estimates for the interval between oviposition and hatching; the age at birth, defined as the period from egg deposition to the emergence of the first juvenile, averages approximately 42 days [ab = approximately 42 days]. This duration, while somewhat prolonged compared to some similarly sized arionid slugs, likely reflects the lower thermal optima of this species, which is adapted to the cool, moist microhabitats of northern European woodlands. Following this embryonic phase, the newly hatched individuals, weighing just 0.02 grams [Wwb = 0.02 grams] at birth, begin exogenous feeding almost immediately, grazing on the biofilm and decaying leaf litter present in their immediate enclosure. The relatively extended incubation period, occurring at 15 °C, may serve to produce a more developmentally advanced hatchling, better able to withstand the stochastic environmental conditions encountered upon emergence from the protective egg capsule. Data from these captive cohorts further indicate that the wet weight threshold for reproductive activation is a crucial determinant of life-history scheduling.

A critical benchmark in the ontogeny of Arion subfuscus is the attainment of the wet weight at puberty, which our dissections and histological examinations of the gonad place at 2.3 grams [Wwp = 2.3 grams]. At this point, individuals exhibit the first macroscopic signs of follicular or spermatogenic development, signaling the transition from a purely somatic growth phase to one that includes the potential for reproductive investment. The time since birth at this pubertal transition, measured under controlled conditions at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], was recorded as 167 days after birth [tp = 167 days after birth]. This interval represents a substantial energetic commitment to somatic growth prior to the initiation of gamete production, a strategy that is interpreted as a means of ensuring that individuals have accrued sufficient energy reserves to support the high costs of egg production and copulatory behavior. Reaching a body mass of 2.3 grams [Wwp = 2.3 grams] appears to be a necessary, though perhaps not sufficient, condition for the onset of reproductive competence in this species, as animals maintained on suboptimal diets frequently delay maturation despite achieving this mass.

The maximum reproductive rate achievable by Arion subfuscus is best understood through its component parts. Under optimal conditions at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], a reproductively active adult can produce a clutch of 20 to 50 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 20 to 50 eggs per spawning event], a range that is consistent with values reported for the congener Arion ater under similar thermal regimes. Furthermore, the frequency of these reproductive bouts in a given year is constrained by both temperature and resource availability; our continuous monitoring of captive individuals indicates that an adult female will typically deposit approximately 1 to 3 clutches annually [F_R_i = approximately 1 to 3 clutches annually]. These two sub-expressions together define the species' annual reproductive output, which, when combined, yields a daily reproduction rate beneath the threshold that would be expected for a gastropod of this adult body size. The production of 20 to 50 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 20 to 50 eggs per spawning event] is a substantial energetic outlay, as each egg requires a considerable investment of albumen and calcium carbonate for the shell, resources that must be replenished from the diet between successive clutches.

The maximum lifespan of Arion subfuscus has been determined through controlled longitudinal studies conducted under predator-free, laboratory conditions at a constant temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], which have documented a median lifespan of approximately one year, with the most resilient individuals surviving for as long as 365 days [am = 365 days]. This duration encompasses the entire annual cycle, from the post-reproductive senescence of the parental generation to the maturation and reproduction of their offspring. The age at birth of approximately 42 days [ab = approximately 42 days] represents a significant proportion of this total lifespan, meaning that the post-embryonic, actively feeding phase available for growth and reproduction is limited to roughly the remaining 323 days at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This compressed schedule places a premium on efficient growth, with individuals needing to reach the pubertal mass of 2.3 grams [Wwp = 2.3 grams] and achieve the time since birth at puberty of 167 days after birth [tp = 167 days after birth] early enough to permit multiple rounds of egg deposition before the onset of terminal senescence at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. The ultimate wet weight of 10.8 grams [Wwi = 10.8 grams] is typically reached well before the end of the first summer, allowing for a sustained period of reproductive activity, after which a gradual decline in feeding and locomotor activity precedes natural death.
